sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the analogy of water for the Torah, emphasizing that just as water descends from a high place to a low place because its true place is below, so too the Torah's true place is below, not above.

translations.translation: And based on this, we can explain what is stated in Tanya39,
after it says that the Holy One, blessed be He, contracted His will and His wisdom and brought them down below,
that therefore the Torah is compared to water40,

for just as water descends from a high place to a low place, so too the Torah descended from its place of honor, which is His will and His wisdom, blessed be He, of which no thought can grasp at all41,
and from there it traveled and descended until it became clothed in physical matters and affairs of this world.
For this requires explanation,
behold, that the Torah descended from above to below is understood even without the analogy of water,
and what is added to the understanding of the matter of the descent of the Torah from above to below by means of the analogy of water?
And we can say the intention in this is,
that just like water,
that they descend from a high place to a low place is because even when they were in a high place they have no connection to that place
(the high place)
where they were found,
and on the contrary, that it is in their nature that they are drawn specifically to a low place indicates their connection, of the water,
(even when they are in a high place)
to the low place,
so too is it with the Torah, which is compared to water,
that this that it descended from above to below is not that its place is above42
and in its descent below it is found not in its place,
but rather,
that its true place
(even when it is above)
is below.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section elaborates that the Torah's descent is like water, which leaves a high place for a low one, unlike the descent of kindness which reveals the giver's quality, and that the Torah rooted in Atzmus was given specifically below.

translations.translation: And we can add,
that this is what is said in Tanya there at the end of the chapter43,
that what is written44
"and His right hand embraces me" refers to the Torah, which is the aspect of kindness and water,
that it specifies kindness and water
(even though to explain the reason for this, that the Torah is called His right hand, it would seemingly suffice to say that it is the aspect of kindness),
it is,
because the drawing down from above to below that is in kindness is in a manner that the high place occupies a place.
And like the influence of a man of kindness,
that in this that he influences his fellow
(drawing down)
the kindness of the influencer is felt.
But unlike the drawing down from above to below of water, which is in a manner that they leave a high place and go
(specifically)
to a low place45.
And this is what it adds, that the Torah is the aspect of
(kindness and)
water,
that this that the Torah descended from above to below is in the likeness of the descent of water46
that leaves a high place,
that the essence of the Torah is specifically below.
And as explained elsewhere47
that this that the Torah is in every place,
above and below48,
is the Torah as it is in the aspect of revelations,
but the Torah as it is rooted in the Awtsmoos was given specifically below.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains "This is the Torah, man," drawing a parallel between the two aspects of man (from above and from the earth) and the two aspects of Torah (its transcendence and its descent specifically below due to its root in Atzmus).

translations.translation: And this is "This is the Torah, man,"
that the Torah is compared to man,
for in man there are two matters.
This that he is called man (Adam) on account of "I will resemble the One above"49,
and this that he is called man (Adam) on account of being formed from the earth (adamah),
as it is brought in the Midrash50
that Adam the first said: I am fitting to be called Adam, for I was created from the earth.
And it is explained in Chassidus51,
that this that Adam the first called his name after the matter
(body)
and not after the form
(soul),
is because Adam the first, in his wisdom, perceived that this that his body was formed from the earth
[inanimate,
and not like other creations whose bodies were from vegetation52],
has in it an advantage also regarding the superiority of his soul,
for everything53
higher, the higher it is, falls lower, the lower it is.
And this is "This is the Torah, man,"
for also in the Torah there are two matters like these.
That this that the Torah is above the world,
to the extent that all worlds are insignificant before it,
is in the manner of the name Adam on account of "I will resemble the One above,"
and this that the Torah descended specifically below, from the aspect that its root is in the Awtsmoos,
is in the manner of the name Adam on account of being formed from the earth, from the aspect that its root is in the higher, the higher it is.
